## How to read this document

This is a course outline, written so that any single section of it can be understood without reading the rest. Every term that isn't everyday English is defined the first time it appears. Two things this document deliberately does not do: it does not explain why any in-class exercise is designed the way it is, and it does not reveal which parts of any exercise are scored versus which are for practice. Those choices exist so the exercises land fresh in the room; they are documented in instructor-only run sheets, not here.

---

## Course description, in one paragraph

Fifty to sixty students per section split into eight teams. Each team claims one real industry and, inside it, makes contact with one real company. Across ten sessions the team builds a deep map of that industry, gets that company's process mapped and one piece of it automated with the company's sign-off, and produces a set of supporting artifacts (marketing collateral, a working app, an automation, a skill, media). Every artifact a student touches, whether built alone or with their team, lands on that student's own live proof-of-work profile on Praxy, which functions as their professional profile going forward. The course is graded on the industry map, the artifacts, the usefulness of what got automated, an individual AI-run interview, peer-assessed contribution, ongoing surprise quizzes, and the quality of the finished Praxy profile itself. The last of those, the profile, is worth at least a quarter of the grade, because a portfolio a stranger can trust is the actual outcome this course exists to produce.

---

## The three pillars

**Judgment.** Deciding what's worth building, which tool fits a given job, and what to trust versus double-check. Taught explicitly through the Operator's Loop and reinforced by the fact that every team's automation must earn a real company contact's approval before it counts.

**Craft.** The hands-on skill of building: prompting, research, using AI to work with data and documents, building an app, automating a workflow, producing media. This is where most class time goes.

**Radar.** Staying current after the course ends. The market for AI tools moves monthly; a student who only learned July 2026's tools has learned a shrinking asset. Carried by the signal desk and by Sessions 7 and 8.

## The Operator's Loop, explained fully

The one method taught in this course that every other exercise assumes you already know. Six steps for any task where you're using AI to get something done:

| Step | In plain words | A concrete example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Frame the problem** | Before touching any tool, write down in one sentence what you're actually trying to solve, and what a good result would look like. | "I need to know which two cities to open a new jewellery store in" is a frame. "Do some research on jewellery" is not. |
| **2. Break it into parts** | Split the problem into smaller pieces, each with one clear job. | City shortlist needs: population of Gen-Z buyers, existing competitor presence, real estate cost, footfall data. |
| **3. Match each part to a capability** | For each piece, name the kind of AI capability it needs: research, writing, image generation, video, data analysis, or automation. | The population and competitor data need research. The cost comparison needs data analysis. |
| **4. Pick your tool and know why** | Choose a specific AI tool or model for each capability, and be able to say why you picked it over an obvious alternative, thinking about cost, speed, privacy, and fit. | "I used a deep-research mode because I needed sources I could check, not a fast guess." |
| **5. Execute and iterate** | Run it. Look at what you got. If it's not good enough, adjust your instructions and run it again. Once is rarely enough. | The first city shortlist missed real estate cost; you re-ran it asking specifically for that. |
| **6. Verify before you trust it** | Before you use the answer for anything real, check the facts, numbers, and sources it gave you. AI states wrong things with the same confidence as right things. | You looked up one cited statistic yourself and found the source didn't say what the AI claimed. |

## The Heist, and what it's for

Session 1 opens with a live simulation exercise called the Heist: a team-based, timed, competitive exercise. What it teaches, and how it connects to the rest of the course, is explained live in the room, not here; instructors have a full script in the Session 1 run sheet. It is not a distraction from the syllabus; it is the first fifty minutes of it.

---

## The industry track: how teams work all course long

**The claim.** In Session 1, each section splits into eight teams of six to eight students. Each team claims one real industry from a curated slate; no industry repeats anywhere in the cohort, so the cohort collectively maps 64+ distinct industries.

**The two things a team builds, across the whole course.**

1. **The value chain map.** A value chain is the full sequence of steps a product or service travels through from raw input to the end customer, including everyone who touches it along the way. A value chain map is that sequence laid out and researched: who the players are at each stage (established companies and startups), how the economics work, what regulations shape the sector, funding environment, public sentiment, hiring in the space, the core jobs, and the global outlook versus India. Built in layers across the term; due in presentable state by Session 6 (checkpoint), delivered in full at the capstone (Sessions 9 and 10).

2. **The company engagement and its automated workflow.** Within their claimed industry, the team identifies one real company (for a jewellery team: an actual brand such as Nivara, Aukera, GIVA, BlueStone, or a competitor). The team makes real contact, maps how a specific part of that business works today, and each member picks one repetitive task within it and builds a working automation for it. The finished automation must be shown to the company contact and receive a real thumbs-up before it counts as complete.

**Supporting artifacts.** Teams also produce a set of artifacts for their chosen company across the term: a jingle, an advertisement, a poster or visual, a skill repo. Everything aims at one real business the team actually knows; nothing is generic practice.

**Individual submission inside team work.** Teams work together and present together, but every artifact is submitted individually by each student to the LMS for evaluation, with their own name on their own piece.

---

## Proof of work: the Praxy profile

Everything a student produces lands on a live profile on Praxy, Praxel's career platform. By the end of the course that profile functions as the student's professional presence: every claim backed by something real, a working app with a link, an automation a real company approved, a published piece, a skill repo on GitHub. Validated by peers and by people outside the course. Worth at least a quarter of the final grade, because "can a stranger trust this without asking questions" is a different skill from "is the underlying work good." Full detail in the companion LMS scoring methodology.

---

## The nine career streams, and where each one's evidence comes from

Masters' Union students choose one of nine specialisations after their first two to three months: Consulting, FOCOS (Founders' Office / General Management / Chief of Staff / Strategy), Product Management, Finance (IB / VC / Corp Fin), HR, Supply Chain and Operations, Sales, Marketing, Data. This course runs before that choice, so it is built to be useful evidence for any stream while letting each student sample the work closest to the stream they're weighing.

| Stream | What in this course looks most like that job | Where the evidence lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consulting | Structuring an unfamiliar industry and building a defensible argument | The value chain map, market and policy layers, the AI interview defence |
| FOCOS | Owning an ambiguous problem end to end, coordinating a team | The company engagement: initiating contact, mapping the process, getting sign-off |
| Product Management | Deciding what's worth building and shipping something that works | The app (Session 4), the automation build (Session 5) |
| Finance | Understanding how a business or sector makes money | The economics layer of the value chain map |
| HR | How work gets divided, staffed, and evaluated | Team formation, the peer scoring process, the hiring-and-jobs layer of the map |
| Supply Chain & Operations | Mapping a real process and finding what can be automated | The company's process map and the resulting automation |
| Sales | Getting a real company to say yes to a meeting, then to finished work | The company outreach and the sign-off |
| Marketing | Telling a company's story so a stranger cares | The jingle, ad, poster, media artifacts |
| Data | Getting a straight, verified answer out of messy real data | Session 3 in full |

## The presentation schedule (for a 50–60 student section)

Eight teams, four hours across Sessions 9 and 10. Reference plan: 20 minutes per team (8 sector deep dive, 7 live artifact demo, 5 questions) = 160 minutes of presenting, leaving 80 for framing, transitions, and close. If more buffer is wanted, 15-minute slots (6/6/3) fit with extra room. Inviting a team's company contact to their slot is recommended where feasible, not required.

---

## Assessment

| Component | What it measures | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value chain map | Depth, breadth, presentation and visual quality of the team's map | 15% |
| Artifact quality | The individual pieces: skill family, data memo, app, media | 15% |
| Workflow relevance and usefulness | Whether the automation solves a real problem, incl. company sign-off | 15% |
| AI interview | A one-on-one AI-run interview on the student's industry and own submissions | 15% |
| Peer contribution | How teammates rate a student's contribution | 10% |
| Continuous evaluation | Unannounced quizzes; best three scores count | 5% |
| Praxy profile | The finished proof-of-work profile as standalone evidence | 25% |

Surprise quizzes are unannounced and run at instructor discretion. Students are told these happen and that their best three count; they are not told which sessions carry one. Full mechanics, bands, and formulas are in the companion LMS scoring methodology.

---

## A note on tools

Specific tools are named as today's best example, not as the syllabus. The capabilities are what's fixed. The exact tool list locks close to delivery, because the market moves monthly and this course would rather teach what's current than what was current when it was written.
